Simple Pixel Art Editor is a free pixel art editor that runs in the browser, with no install or account needed. It covers sprite drawing with layers, mirror drawing and selections, frame-by-frame animation with onion skin and frame tags, and exports to PNG, GIF and sprite sheets.

It also includes tools for game assets: a tileset editor that generates Wang-16 and blob-47 auto-tile terrains from a base tile and exports Godot 4 TileSet (.tres) and Tiled (.tsx) files, a tilemap painter with an isometric mode, a palette library and an image-to-pixel-art converter.

It suits beginners and hobbyists making sprites and tilesets for small 2D games. The source code is MIT-licensed. [...] Resprite is a pixel art and animation editor for iOS, Android, Windows and macOS, built around a touch interface without losing the tools a desktop editor has: pixel-perfect lines, alpha lock, dithering patterns, custom brushes, gradients and symmetry. It imports and exports GIF, sprite sheets, PSD and APNG.

Pixelorama is a full featured free editor: layers, animation with onion skinning, tile mode, palettes, and an active development pace. It runs on every desktop platform and in the browser.

GraphicsGale has been in use since 2005 and excels at animation, with onion skinning and frame-by-frame preview. It was made freeware in 2017. The interface shows its age but the tools are precise. [...] Warning: a modern web browser is required to use this website.

We detected that you may have an out of date or unsupported web browser. This tool, like many others on this site and across the web uses features only available in new web browsers. We reccommend updating your current browser or downloading Firefox or Chrome.

Aseprite is a pixel art editor built around sprite work: an indexed-color workflow, onion skinning and a timeline for animation, tilemap layers, custom brushes, and export straight to sprite sheets. Extensions and Lua scripts add anything it lacks. It is the editor most Lospec artists reach for first.

## Wrapping Up

In my personal experience, the two strongest applications on this list are Pyxel Edit and Aseprite, and I don’t feel you can really separate which of the two is “best”. This is because if you are involved in game development and the creation of tilesets you’ll find Pyxel Edit’s specialization very helpful. But if you’re a character and animation artist, you’ll find Aseprite’s specialization very helpful. [...] Both applications can do some of what the other specializes in, though I’d say Pyxel Edit is probably stronger in animation than Aseprite is strong in tileset creation. However Aseprite is probably stronger for self contained artwork creation than Pyxel Edit. Overall I’d suggest if you’re involved in multiple types of pixel art, using the two together might serve you well.

I would class Piskel as a great application for when you want to get something done fast, or for when you’re on the move and need to access a quality pixel art editor online. [...] The focus of Piskel is definitely sprite creation and animation as opposed to tilesets or complete scene creation. It has a relatively limited set of tools, but it also has a direct approach that can be very efficient for sprite creation and animation. It’s made particularly convenient given it has a fully fledged online version, meaning you can access it anywhere.

After drawing your initial character sprite, animations are created easily by just hitting the Add new frame button to the left of the canvas and adjusting an FPS slider to control your speed. Onion skinning is included, which is always a valuable feature in animation.
